title: Teenager's hand blown off during confrontation between France school protesters and police
content: A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators near a school in France, an official has said, as student protests continue across the country. The "very serious incident" happened in the northern city of Lens on Monday morning, according to the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, François-Xavier Lauch. "The student's life is not in danger," he said, adding that the teenager was transferred "very quickly" to a hospital nearby. Around 500 schools were partially or totally closed across the country on Monday amid student protests over the condition of school buildings and staffing which have led to clashes with police in recent days. There are mixed reports in French media about how the boy came to sustain the injury. The AFP news agency, citing a police union source, reported that the student appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which exploded in his hand. However, regional newspaper La Voix Du Nord quoted a girl, who was reportedly standing near the teenager, as saying he did not pick up the grenade. "He didn't pick it up. I was there, I saw it. He didn't pick it up, he didn't catch it," she was quoted as saying. When asked about the incident, Lens Mayor Sylvain Robert said the circumstances still needed to be clarified. "Like you, and like many others, I have seen some videos showing the aftermath. But I did not see how the operation was organised, either by the police or by the students," he told French media. A regional prosecutor said an investigation would be carried out by the French police watchdog, the General Inspection of the National Police (IGPN), "so all light can be shed on what happened". The incident took place close to the Auguste Béhal high school, the prefect said. Lauch said a "larger gathering" of students than on previous days had assembled outside the school. "At the start of the morning, they threw various projectiles at the local police officers who were on site initially. When I say projectiles, I mean stones, fireworks, and mortars," he told French media. "Instructions were given by the interdepartmental director of the National Police, naturally with my approval, to deploy a company of riot police (CRS) here to maintain order, and it was in this context that this event occurred." The school issued a statement on Monday morning, saying: "In light of the events that took place this morning and in order to ensure the safety of the entire school community, the institution is switching to distance learning from now on. "In addition, to support everyone during this period, a listening and support unit has also been set up at the establishment." According to education minister Édouard Geffray, at least 190 students have been injured since the protests began. Last week, Eden, 14, was badly hurt in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône after reportedly being struck in the head by a tear gas grenade. The student suffered "a double jaw fracture" and had to undergo "extremely major surgery", according to his lawyer. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has announced an investigation. Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Eden's mother said her heart was "shattered". "His jaw is wired shut. He can't eat except through a straw and only liquids," French media outlet BFMTV reported her as saying. "It's shameful, it's appalling, it's violent, it's horrific," she said, adding: "This should not happen. They are dealing with children who are asking for better conditions in which to study." The recent wave of protests began in late September in Paris and has spread across the country. High school students started the demonstrations, complaining about a lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. University students joined last week, making similar demands. More than 5,000 people have been arrested altogether since the start of the movement, according to AFP, with around 85% of them minors. The radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon described the protests as the "most powerful high school and university student youth movement" since 1968 - a major year of French protest, which saw millions of workers go on strike. Education minister Geffray said Monday saw a "clear decrease" in the number of schools disrupted compared to recent days, with 589 institutions affected. Last Friday, French authorities said 735 of France's 3,700 schools had been disrupted. But France is braced for more large protests on Tuesday, as student organisation Union Syndicale Lycéenne (USL) has again called on people to take to the streets. Other organisations, including the teachers' union SNES-FSU, have also shown their support for the students, urging their members to join tomorrow's protest. In response, the French government said it would set up a "major consultation platform" for students from across the country to share details of the difficulties they have experienced. Geffray said he hoped to resolve "most of the problematic situations" by 16 October. Calling of a snap election was not a knee-jerk reaction from Pedro Sánchez but a carefully thought-out manoeuvre, Guy Hedgecoe reports from Madrid. Sánchez says Spain will head to the polls on 29 November after recent defeats on measures aimed at addressing the country's housing crisis. A series of measures to tackle the housing crisis were defeated in parliament on Friday Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez says the situation in Catalonia remains "very complicated". title: Zelensky condemns 'horrific' Russian strike on boat carrying corn in Black Sea
content: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has condemned a "horrific" Russian attack on a vessel carrying corn in the Black Sea. The ship's captain was killed in the strike involving two drones, Zelensky said, and another sailor was unaccounted for. Eleven crew members - nationals of Azerbaijan and India - have been rescued. Romania said it had mounted a rescue mission after "a fire on the ship Royad Mammadov" outside the country's territorial waters. It said two people had died. Russia has not commented, but its defence ministry earlier said it had struck two cargo vessels. Russia has been pounding Ukrainian infrastructure in what it says is retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries and ships in the Black Sea. Monday's attack by Russia targeted "a civilian vessel in neutral waters carrying corn and owned by Turkey", Volodymyr Zelensky said. He did not give the location of the ship, but Romania's interior ministry said it had sunk about 30 nautical miles south of its port of Sfantu Gheorghe. "At around 11:00 (09:00 GMT), Coast Guard border police officers were informed that a fire had broken out on board a commercial vessel located within Romania's exclusive economic zone," the ministry said in a statement. "Eleven crew members have been rescued. Two deceased persons have also been identified," it added. Ukraine's president said he had "repeatedly proposed concrete steps to de-escalate the situation and ensure security in the Black Sea" - and other countries had made "relevant proposals" too. "But Russia consistently chooses terror and sinking civilian vessels instead of normal maritime navigation," Zelensky said. "Pressure is needed to restore global food security," he added. "And everyone who is genuinely interested in this must help." On Sunday, Russia's defence ministry said it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier last week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helped the Kremlin finance the war which began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. President Vladimir Putin admitted last week Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. The Russian leader has also intensified his rhetoric against Western allies of Ukraine - repeating a threat of even using nuclear weapons . Western allies have faced a surge in so-called hybrid warfare incidents blamed on Russia, particularly in Poland and the Baltics in recent months. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said last Thursday that his country was preparing for further hybrid attacks, "including serious ones", after a drone armed with explosives was found in August on the tarmac at Leipzig airport close to Ukrainian cargo planes. The head of Germany's foreign intelligence Martin Jaeger said on Monday that "Germany is in danger of becoming embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia", which was "waging a shadow war" with the threat of attacks against targets in Germany remaining "real and imminent". The strike on the Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge comes after repeat attacks on another major bridge in Ukraine's capital. The town council is looking into the possibility of twinning with Okhtyrka as a show of support. Northern Ireland captain Trai Hume and men's top goal scorer David Healy have their say on Ruari McConville unselfishly allowing Ciaron Brown's header to trickle over the line in NI's 3-0 win over Ukraine in the Nations League. Watch highlights as Northern Ireland produce a ruthless display to beat Ukraine 3-0 in their Uefa Nations League game in Trnava. title: Pentagon stops using Anthropic AI tools after blacklisting company, BBC told
content: The US Department of Defence is no longer using Anthropic's AI tools, an official has told the BBC, months after it designated the company a supply chain risk on national security grounds. The Pentagon "has ceased the use of Anthropic products", the department official said in a statement on Monday. Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth labelled Anthropic a supply chain risk in February, and announced that the Pentagon would stop using it by late August. It is not clear why there has been a delay. Multiple people familiar with the matter told the BBC that as recently as last week Anthopic's Claude model was still being used by the department in research, analysis and intelligence gathering as well as in military operations against Iran. It was viewed as a critical tool for sorting through vast quantities of information, the people said. They include former US defence officials and contractors who have worked closely with the Pentagon specifically on AI. A spokesman for Anthropic declined to comment when asked about the Pentagon's statement. The details of the department stopping all use of Anthropic's tools have not been previously reported. The firm had been used by the US government and military since 2024 and was the first advanced AI company to have its tools deployed in government agencies doing classified work. But earlier this year, the Pentagon pressed it to remove its safety guardrails from Claude and give the military unfettered access to its AI products. When Anthropic refused, citing concerns of mass surveillance and autonomous weapons, Hegseth designated the company a "national security supply-chain risk" - a law typically reserved for companies based in countries that pose a threat to the US. Anthropic said the move was "unprecedented and unlawful" and has sued the Trump administration in an effort to overturn the designation. As this legal fight has played out in the courts, the Pentagon has signed contracts with other major tech companies, including Google, xAI and OpenAI. OpenAI tools have been more widely adopted in recent months in some military departments, according to two people familiar with AI use in the defence department The Pentagon's statement on Monday came in response to a question from the BBC about its use of Anthropic, after multiple people said in interviews that Claude was still being widely used. It was embedded in a larger data platform used by the Pentagon called Maven Smart System, multiple sources said. Maven, which is operated by Palantir, is the Pentagon's primary platform for organising intelligence and other data. Lauren Kahn, a senior research analyst at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology said that because Claude was deeply integrated into Maven it would have been difficult to remove it quickly from the system. "The fact that it took the Pentagon until now to remove all use of Claude from across the system is indicative that these things are not just plug and play," she said. "Once they become integrated it can be painful to remove them," added Kahn, a former US defence official. The BBC spoke with defence contractors who specialise in AI and have worked closely with the Pentagon, as well as former US defence officials and others familiar with the Pentagon's use of artificial intelligence. Several spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media. When Hegseth initially ordered Anthropic to be phased out of government, "there was concern with moving beyond Anthropic to OpenAI" and other tools, a former senior US defence official said. Hegseth set a six-month deadline to phase out Anthropic on 27 February, one day before the US and Israel attacked Iran. Pentagon employees continued to use Anthropic's Claude tools, including its powerful Mythos models, "throughout the whole period of the controversy" with the company, one of the people said. Claude was used in particular for intelligence gathering and analysis, including through Palantir's Maven system, several sources said. Palantir, a leading defence tech firm, was founded by the billionaire ally of President Donald Trump, Peter Thiel. Sources familiar with the way the technology is used said analysts and other defence officials rely on Maven to access and organise visual data, including satellite imagery and drone footage. The data was then fed into Claude and other large language models for tasks such as identifying potential military targets. Officials frequently used the technology when compiling one-page briefs that were passed up the chain of command, according to a source who was given a demonstration of Maven by Palantir earlier this year. Maven is also used by some US allies to share intelligence with the Trump administration. Anthropic's clash with the Pentagon comes as relations with the White House appear to be warming. Trump met with Anthropic boss Dario Amodei twice at the White House last week. After one of the meetings with Trump and other technology leaders, Amodei said he still had concerns about risks posed by AI. "How we address those risks is still under discussion," Amodei told reporters at the White House, as Trump stood by his side, but "if we work with the president, we can win safely". Trump then proceeded to praise Amodei, saying he was "great" and "fantastic." Sign up for our Tech Decoded newsletter to follow the world's top tech stories and trends. Outside the UK? Sign up here .
